entry.title: Identifying Discrete-State Network Dynamics
entry.content:
Speaker: Carolyn L. Beck, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
Date: October 23, 2026
Series: Purdue ICON Weekly Seminar / ECE Distinguished Lecture

The lecture asked how to identify a networked dynamical system when its observed states take only discrete values. The main goal was to recover network weights and topology from binary time series, with guarantees on the estimation error after a finite number of observations.

These notes are based on two partial transcripts and four slide screenshots. A middle segment was not recorded, so the summary covers the available material without reconstructing the missing discussion.

From binary observations to network structure

Examples included opinion dynamics, epidemic spread, gene regulation, and cascading defaults in financial networks. In each case, a node’s state can depend on its neighbors’ earlier states. The identification problem is to infer those interactions from the observed evolution of the network.

For a network with $p$ binary nodes, the full state space has $2^p$ elements. Estimating an unrestricted Markov transition matrix therefore involves exponentially many entries. The lecture instead used a Bernoulli autoregressive (BAR) model, which expresses each node’s activation probability through a weighted combination of the previous network state and a noise contribution.

After combining the noise parameters into an offset, the conditional activation probability has the form

\[\Pr\!\left(X_i(k+1)=1\mid X(k)\right) =a_i^{\mathsf T}X(k)+c_i.\]

Here, $a_i$ contains the incoming network weights for node $i$. Together, the weight matrix and offsets have $p^2+p$ parameters. Parameter constraints keep the probabilities valid. In the basic nonnegative-influence model, persistent noise prevents the process from remaining trapped at an all-zero or all-one state and supports identification.

This is a structured model of the transition dynamics: the reduction in parameters comes from the BAR assumptions, rather than from an ability to estimate any arbitrary Markov chain with the same amount of data.

Consistency and the two estimators

The talk distinguished strong consistency from sample complexity. Consistency asks whether an estimator converges to the true parameters as the observation horizon grows without bound. Sample complexity asks how many observations suffice for a specified error with high probability.

The lecture considered the direct maximum likelihood estimator and a closed-form estimator. Empirical state and transition counts supply estimates of conditional probabilities; the BAR structure then relates these probabilities to the network parameters through linear equations. The displayed closed-form construction uses a Gram-matrix inverse.

The finite-sample analysis presented later concerned the closed-form estimator. The speaker identified corresponding sample-complexity guarantees for the direct maximum likelihood estimator as an open problem.

What controls the number of observations?

One slide gave a sufficient sample-size requirement on the scale

\[\frac{p^3\log p} {(1-r)^2\epsilon^2\lambda_{\min}(\Pi)^2}\]

to obtain $\lVert\widehat{\Theta}-\Theta_0\rVert_F<\epsilon$ with high probability, under the stated model assumptions. The quantities have distinct roles:

  • Network dimension $p$: larger networks require more observations.
  • Target error $\epsilon$: a smaller error tolerance increases the sample requirement.
  • Dobrushin coefficient $r$: this describes dependence and contraction of the process. As $r$ approaches one, the dependence makes the bound less favorable.
  • Correlation matrix $\Pi$: this is the second-moment matrix of the state augmented with a constant. A small minimum eigenvalue indicates poor conditioning for parameter estimation.

The interpretation of $r$ was how quickly the process forgets its earlier conditions. This matters because consecutive observations are dependent; a long trajectory cannot simply be treated as equally many independent samples.

The requirement is a conservative sufficient condition, obtained by bounding the estimation error. It does not establish a matching lower bound on the number of samples every estimator must use. This distinction also came up in the questions after the talk.

How the proof separates the difficulties

The slides bounded the spectral-norm estimation error by a ratio: a random error term in the numerator and the minimum eigenvalue of a data Gram matrix in the denominator. The proof therefore needs an upper bound on the numerator and a positive lower bound on the denominator, both holding with high probability.

For the denominator, the argument rescales the data matrix using its expected second moments and controls how far the resulting Gram matrix deviates from the identity. Since the observations form a dependent process, this requires concentration results for Markov chains rather than a direct independent-sample argument.

For the numerator, the slides used a matrix Freedman inequality. The error can be expressed through a martingale difference sequence, allowing matrix concentration bounds to control it. Combining the two estimates yields the finite-sample guarantee.

Applications and open directions

The reported simulations suggested that the theoretical sample requirement could be conservative. Gene-signaling examples also involved positive and negative influences. More recent work explored dependencies in waterway transportation networks, including seasonal usage of locks.

The lecture closed with several directions for further work: tighter bounds, guarantees for the direct likelihood estimator, and the use of known network structure. For example, physical geography can rule out particular connections in a waterway network. Such information, or assumptions about sparsity and maximum degree, could reduce the identification burden.

Other extensions included partial observation, states with more than two values, and alternative estimators. The presentation’s main analysis assumed that all node states were observed over time.

Related paper

Xiaotian Xie, Dimitrios Katselis, Carolyn L. Beck, and R. Srikant. Finite Sample Analysis for Structured Discrete System Identification. IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, 68(10), 6345–6352, 2023. The paper gives the formal assumptions and results behind the finite-sample analysis.
entry.summary: ICON seminar notes on Bernoulli autoregressive models, network identification, and finite-sample estimation guarantees.

entry.title: Learning Causal Graphs with Mixed-Integer Optimization

link.title: Learning Causal Graphs with Mixed-Integer Optimization

entry.content:
Speaker: Simge Küçükyavuz, Northwestern University
Date: October 16, 2026
Series: Optimization seminar, Purdue University

The seminar discussed how optimization can help learn directed graphical models from observational data. The main setting was a linear Gaussian structural equation model, with particular attention to the case where different variables have different noise variances. The talk connected three ideas: a convex mixed-integer formulation, an early stopping rule guided by statistical accuracy, and a coordinate descent method for larger problems.

Learning a graph from data

The opening example involved exercise, body weight, and heart health. Observations may reveal relationships among these variables, but learning a directed graph requires deciding which relationships exist and how they are oriented. The model considered in the talk represents these relationships with a directed acyclic graph (DAG).

Each variable is expressed as a linear combination of its parents plus a noise term. Learning the model therefore means estimating both the graph structure and the coefficients on its edges. The objective combines a negative log-likelihood with an L0 penalty, which counts nonzero edge coefficients and encourages a sparse graph. An acyclicity constraint rules out directed cycles.

A key distinction was between equal and unequal noise variances. Equal variances can make the graph identifiable under suitable assumptions. With unequal variances, observational data generally cannot determine every edge direction uniquely. The appropriate target is then a Markov equivalence class: a collection of DAGs that encode the same conditional independencies. A completed partially directed acyclic graph (CPDAG) represents this class, showing which directions are shared across its members and which remain unresolved.

A convex mixed-integer formulation

The original likelihood formulation contains difficult interactions between the edge coefficients and noise variances. The speaker described a change of variables based on a factorization of the precision matrix, the inverse covariance matrix.

The DAG structure is useful here: there exists a simultaneous permutation of rows and columns that makes the relevant matrix triangular. This allows a log-determinant expression to be rewritten using scalar logarithms of diagonal entries. The resulting formulation has a convex continuous objective, together with discrete decisions that encode the graph.

Binary variables indicate whether edges are present. They also make it possible to count edges for the L0 penalty. Layer variables enforce acyclicity by requiring a selected edge to move forward in the layer ordering. The formulation can incorporate a candidate superstructure to restrict the search, as well as prior knowledge about particular relationships. The talk also mentioned perspective strengthening as a way to improve continuous relaxations.

Stopping at a statistically meaningful accuracy

Branch and bound maintains a lower bound from relaxations and an upper bound from feasible solutions. Their difference measures the remaining optimization gap. Finding a good graph may be much faster than proving that no better graph exists.

The seminar connected this gap to the statistical properties of the estimator. Under the stated assumptions, an appropriately chosen stopping threshold can preserve consistency without requiring the solver to close the gap completely. The threshold depends on statistical quantities such as regularization and sparsity.

The experiments illustrated the tradeoff: a suitable early stopping rule reduced computation while maintaining estimation quality, whereas stopping with too large a gap could reduce accuracy. A practical complication discussed in the questions was that the true graph sparsity is unknown and must be estimated when applying the rule.

Coordinate descent for larger problems

For larger graphs, the talk introduced a coordinate descent algorithm. It updates one entry of the transformed parameter matrix at a time while keeping the others fixed. An update that would create a directed cycle is excluded.

The method has convergence guarantees to a coordinate-wise minimum. Under the paper’s assumptions, its objective value also approaches the optimal penalized likelihood value as the sample size grows, with finite-sample statistical guarantees. This asymptotic result does not imply that every finite-data run finds a globally optimal solution.

The reported experiments compared computation time and differences between estimated and true CPDAGs. They showed the benefits of accounting for unequal noise variances and the speed of coordinate descent on larger benchmark networks. The discussion also highlighted the importance of the coordinate update order.

Further discussion

The closing discussion covered using expert knowledge or interventions to resolve ambiguous directions, extending the model beyond the linear Gaussian setting, and exploiting structure in sparse quadratic optimization problems. One computational distinction was that the data enter the formulation through a sample covariance matrix: increasing the sample size does not directly add graph-decision variables, while increasing the number of nodes or candidate edges expands the combinatorial search.

Related papers

These notes summarize the seminar rather than reproduce its proofs. The following papers provide the precise assumptions and guarantees behind the two main methods:

  • Tong Xu, Armeen Taeb, Simge Küçükyavuz, and Ali Shojaie. Integer programming for learning directed acyclic graphs from nonidentifiable Gaussian models. Biometrika, 2025.
  • Tong Xu, Simge Küçükyavuz, Ali Shojaie, and Armeen Taeb. An Asymptotically Optimal Coordinate Descent Algorithm for Learning Bayesian Networks from Gaussian Models.
entry.summary: Seminar notes on DAG learning, statistically motivated early stopping, and coordinate descent.
